hook.text: Every line between two tables ends on a row. So how do you say WHICH row?

taylors.text: Two customers named Taylor Kim, both in Portland. An order for coffee beans says Taylor Kim. Which one?

blink.text: With no key, Postgres can't tell. It'll store the same row twice.

ids.text: A primary key fixes that: customer one oh one, and customer one oh two.

rules.text: And Postgres holds a key to two rules: unique, and never null.

dup.text: Customer one is Ada. Add Grace as customer one too, and it's refused. Key one already exists.

null.text: Leave the ID off? Refused again. No pointer can mean maybe this one, maybe that one.

roster.text: A key can be two columns. In a roster, student seven takes two courses, and course forty-two has two students.

pair.text: Neither ID is unique, but the pair is: seven in forty-two, only once.

stable.text: And a key should almost never change, because other tables point at it.

kinds-in.text: So what should a key be?

kinds.text: A natural key is a value the thing already has, like a country code. See J P, and you know it's Japan.

surrogate.text: A surrogate key is a number the database makes up, just to name the row. It means nothing... on purpose.

wallet.text: Why bother? In nineteen thirty-eight, a wallet maker in Lockport, New York, put a sample Social Security card in every wallet.

real.text: It carried a real person's number, and buyers adopted it. By nineteen forty-three, over five thousand people were using it.

broke.text: One unique number, shared by thousands, and the permanent one got cancelled. A natural key bets on promises you don't control.

email.text: It goes wrong quietly, too. Make email the key, and when Ada changes hers, Postgres refuses: her order still points at the old one.

user-ten.text: Make her user ten instead, and the change just goes through. Keep email unique, just not the key.

fk-in.text: So a key names a row. Now, let's point at one.

fk.text: An order belongs to a customer, so it stores the customer's key, in customer ID. That's a foreign key.

parent.text: The table it points at is the parent. The one holding the pointer is the child.

many.text: It lives on the many side, and it copies nothing else. Just the ID.

defend.text: Postgres checks that line. An order for customer one goes right in.

ninety.text: Customer ninety-nine doesn't exist, so that order's rejected. It would've been an orphan, a child whose parent isn't there.

ri-in.text: But what happens when a parent leaves?

delete.text: Referential integrity means every pointer points at something real. So deleting a parent forces a choice.

restrict.text: Restrict blocks it. Ada Co still has an invoice, so the account stays.

cascade.text: Cascade takes the children along. Delete the spam post, and BOTH its comments go too.

setnull.text: And set null keeps the child but clears the pointer. Sam leaves, and his ticket stays, assigned to no one.

choose.text: So which? Ask what the child means without its parent. Nothing? Cascade. Can it stand alone? Set null. A record you must keep? Restrict.

update.text: Changing a parent's key asks the same question... one more reason to pick a key that never changes.

next.text: And with keys to point with, you can build every shape a relationship takes.
